name: Good AI Practice in Manufacturing
blurb: The FDA and EMA principles applied to production.
title: Good AI Practice in Manufacturing
answer: The ten FDA and EMA principles of good AI practice explicitly include manufacturing. For plants this means risk based use, high quality data, documented models, and monitoring through the product lifecycle.

reading.body:
The FDA and EMA's ten principles of good AI practice cover manufacturing, and they add no new binding rules, only the expectation that existing GMP applies to AI.

That distinction is the practical content here. A plant adopting AI does not face a separate regulatory regime. It faces the same regime read through AI: risk based use, high quality data, documented models, and monitoring across the product lifecycle. The principles are guidance on how existing requirements land on these systems, not a new layer above them.

The recommended home for them is the site quality manual and its procedures, so that every AI project inherits the same expectations by default. That matters because the alternative is per project governance, rebuilt each time and hard for an inspector to recognise. Writing the principles into the manual also settles the question of where accountability sits, which is the plant, not the vendor or the model.

What this does not cover is the substance of validation, data integrity, or specific applications such as inspection, predictive maintenance, or digital twins. Those are separate subjects. Nor does the data say how the principles are enforced, what an inspector will ask for, or how the FDA and EMA differ in emphasis. It establishes that manufacturing is in scope and where the rules should live, and stops there.

The principles are guidance on how existing GMP applies to AI, which means the compliance work is not a new submission but a mapping exercise. A plant has to show where each of the ten principles lands in procedures it already runs, and the data names the areas that mapping touches: risk based use, representative and well governed data, documentation of how models were built and tested, performance assessment in the actual operating context, lifecycle monitoring, and operator information about what a system does and its limits.

Writing them into the site quality manual changes the default. A new AI project inherits the expectations rather than negotiating them, and an inspector sees a structure already familiar from the rest of the manual. The data frames this as the difference between governance that is inherited and governance that is rebuilt per project.

What the data does not supply is the enforcement side. It states that the principles create no binding rules and that they show how regulators expect existing GMP to be applied, but it does not say what an inspector will ask for, how the two agencies differ in emphasis, or how any of this is checked in practice.

Do the principles add new requirements for a manufacturing plant?
No. They do not create binding rules, but they show how regulators expect existing GMP to be applied to AI.

Where should the principles be written down?
In the site quality manual and procedures, so all AI projects follow them.

Which parts of a plant's operation do the principles actually reach?
Risk based use, high quality data, documented models, and monitoring through the product lifecycle, plus assessment of performance in the actual operating context and clear information to operators about what a system does and its limits.

Does the data cover validation, data integrity, or specific applications like inspection and predictive maintenance?
No. It establishes that manufacturing is in scope and where the rules should live, and stops there.

How are the principles enforced, and what will an inspector ask for?
The data does not hold this. It says only that the principles are not binding rules.

Do the FDA and EMA differ in emphasis?
The data does not say. It records that the two agencies issued the principles jointly in January 2026 and treats them as one set.

explainer:
The FDA and EMA principles apply to manufacturing as much as to clinical work. In a plant they translate into concrete practices: decide where AI is justified by assessing risk, use representative and well governed data, document how models were built and tested, assess performance in the actual operating context, monitor through the lifecycle, and give operators clear information about what a system does and its limits.

Building these into the site quality manual and standard procedures means every new AI project inherits them by default rather than reinventing governance each time, and it gives inspectors a recognisable structure.

What good practice means on a production floor

Good manufacturing practice already requires that every process affecting product quality be defined, controlled and documented. AI does not get an exception. A model that adjusts a process setting, predicts a batch outcome or decides whether a vial passes inspection is part of the process, so the same questions apply: what does it do, how was it shown to work, who is responsible when it is wrong, and what happens when it changes?

The four controls that keep coming up

First, intended use: a written statement of exactly what the model decides, on what data, within what range, and what it never decides. Second, a human in control: for anything that releases product or changes a critical parameter, a qualified person confirms the action, and the system makes that easy rather than a formality. Third, lifecycle management: models drift as raw materials, equipment and seasons change, so there is a plan for monitoring performance, retraining, revalidating and retiring. Fourth, records: inputs, outputs, versions and overrides are captured so a deviation can be investigated months later.

Why manufacturers move slowly

A validated line that works is expensive to change, and every change invites inspection questions. So most plants introduce AI first in advisory roles, such as flagging a trend for an operator, and only move it into the control loop once they have months of evidence that it agrees with the people. That is cautious, but it is also how the industry has always adopted automation, and it produces the records regulators ask for.
